claim: Any construction within a runway approach surface requires notice to the FAA on Form 7460-1 under 14 CFR 77.9, triggering an obstruction evaluation/airspace analysis that ends in an FAA Determination of No Hazard or Hazard.
source_title: 14 CFR Part 77 — Safe, Efficient Use, and Preservation of the Navigable Airspace
supporting_excerpt: If required to file notice under 14 CFR Part 77 § 77.9, an applicant must submit a completed FAA Form 7460-1, Notice of Proposed Construction or Alteration.
caveat: The obstruction-evaluation gate is independent of MWAA's internal planning review; a Determination of Hazard does not by itself legally bar construction but is a mandatory federal finding.

claim: Section 163 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 limited the FAA's authority over on-airport land use to development that (A) materially impacts the safe and efficient operation of aircraft, (B) adversely affects safety of people/property on the ground, or (C) adversely affects the value of prior Federal investments to a significant extent.
source_title: FAA Releases Guidance on Section 163 and Limited Federal Control Over Airport Property
supporting_excerpt: FAA generally retains authority to regulate activities that: (1) 'materially impact the safe and efficient operation of aircraft at, to, or from the airport,' (2) 'adversely affect the safety of people or property on the ground as a result of aircraft operations', or (3) 'adversely affect the value of prior Federal investments to a significant extent.'
data_vintage: 2018 statute; guidance 2020, revised by Sec. 743 in 2024
caveat: The three prongs match the (A)/(B)/(C) test quoted in the author's memo. Section 163 cuts both ways: it was intended to reduce FAA friction on non-aeronautical revenue development. Section 743 of the 2024 reauthorization revised Section 163.

claim: The FAA has a December 8, 2023 policy specifically governing processing of land-use changes on federally acquired or federally conveyed airport land.
source_title: Policy Regarding Processing Land Use Changes on Federally Acquired or Federally Conveyed Airport Land
supporting_excerpt: Policy Regarding Processing Land Use Changes on Federally Acquired or Federally Conveyed Airport Land
airport_or_entity: FAA / sponsors on federally conveyed land
caveat: Full policy text not fetched (FAA.gov 403); cited from Federal Register listing. Applies to Dulles because DOT holds title to the land.

claim: Grant Assurance 20 (Hazard Removal and Mitigation) is based on 49 U.S.C. 47107(a)(9) and requires the sponsor to mitigate hazards including those identified by the FAA Form 7460-1 obstruction evaluation.
source_title: Order 5190.6C, Appendix A — Airport Sponsors Assurances; and Chapter 20 Compatible Land Use
supporting_excerpt: Grant Assurance 20, Hazard Removal and Mitigation, is based on 49 U.S.C. § 47107(a)(9). The sponsor must take appropriate action to mitigate hazards including those identified by FAA Form 7460-1 obstruction evaluation.
caveat: Exact verbatim assurance text not fetched (FAA.gov 403); statutory basis and gist confirmed via search summary of 5190.6C and 2025 assurances form.

claim: 49 U.S.C. 47107(a)(9) requires appropriate action to clear and protect terminal airspace required to protect instrument and visual operations by mitigating existing and preventing future airport hazards.
source_title: 49 U.S.C. § 47107 — Project grant application approval conditioned on assurances
supporting_excerpt: appropriate action will be taken to ensure that terminal airspace required to protect instrument and visual operations to the airport (including operations at established minimum flight altitudes) will be cleared and protected by mitigating existing, and preventing future, airport hazards

claim: 49 U.S.C. 47107(a)(10) (basis for Grant Assurance 21, Compatible Land Use) requires appropriate action, including zoning, to restrict use of land near the airport to uses compatible with normal airport operations.
supporting_excerpt: appropriate action, including the adoption of zoning laws, has been or will be taken to the extent reasonable to restrict the use of land next to or near the airport to uses that are compatible with normal airport operations
caveat: GA 21 addresses land 'near the airport'; on-airport uses are also governed by ALP/GA 29 and Section 163.

claim: FAA AC 150/5200-33C recommends siting hazardous-wildlife attractants at least 10,000 feet from any runway used by turbine-powered aircraft, and that stormwater detention basins remain totally dry between rainfalls (or be paved) to avoid creating wildlife habitat.
source_title: AC 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants On or Near Airports
supporting_excerpt: FAA recommends that wildlife-attracting uses be located beyond 10,000 feet for airports serving turbine-powered aircraft... detention basins should remain totally dry between rainfalls, and where constant flow of water is anticipated... the detention facility should include a concrete or paved pad and/or ditch/swale in the bottom to prevent vegetation that may provide nesting habitat.
caveat: The author's memo cited the prior '33' designation; current version is 33C. A wet retention pond adjacent to the departure/landing corridor is the attractant of concern.

claim: The FAA treats thermal exhaust plumes as a potential aircraft hazard and has published a technical guidance and assessment tool (based on MITRE's Exhaust-Plume-Analyzer), but characterizes the overall risk of flight disruption as low, significant mainly to light aircraft in calm/cold/unstable conditions.
source_title: Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations: Technical Guidance and Assessment Tool
supporting_excerpt: The FAA has determined the overall risk associated with thermal exhaust plumes in causing a disruption of flight is low, however thermal exhaust plumes in the vicinity of airports may pose a unique hazard to aircraft in critical phases of flight (particularly takeoff, landing and within the pattern). Studies predict that the significant turbulent effects of an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower.
caveat: The 4.3 m/s vertical-velocity threshold sometimes cited is an Australian CASA figure, NOT an FAA standard. Use plume point as 'unassessed unknown' requiring analysis, not as proven hazard.

claim: The 4.3 m/s plume vertical-velocity hazard threshold is an Australian CASA-derived figure, not an FAA standard; its original basis has reportedly been lost and CASA uses it only as a screening trigger.
source_title: CASA Advisory Circular 139.E-02 Plume rise assessments (and related analyses)
supporting_excerpt: CASA may determine that plume velocities in excess of 4.3 m/s is or will be a potential hazard to aircraft operations. However, the basis of the original CASA derived threshold of 4.3 m/s has been lost... an additional more rigorous analysis... should be used if the 4.3 m/s and 10.6 m/s screening thresholds are exceeded at altitudes that have the potential to affect aviation.
denominator: vertical plume velocity at assessment altitude
caveat: Cited to prevent mis-attribution to the FAA. Useful only as evidence that a numeric plume standard is contested internationally.

claim: MWAA sold 424 acres of Dulles 'Western Lands' to data-center developer Digital Realty for $236.5 million (about $558K/acre), now the 'Digital Dulles' campus, explicitly to hold down the future cost per enplaned passenger.
source_title: The Airports Authority Announces Sale of 424 Acres of Western Lands at Dulles International
supporting_excerpt: The final sale price of $236.5 million... The sale of the Western Lands generated significant non-aeronautical revenue for the Airports Authority, which was instrumental in the mission to hold down the future cost per enplaned passenger at Dulles International.
caveat: Western Lands were peripheral parcels outside the runway surfaces — distinguishable from the proposed data center inside RWY 19R/1L surfaces. Net proceeds figure (~$207M) also cited in reporting.

claim: MWAA adopted a new Dulles master plan in July 2025; airlines formally concurred on July 15, 2026; and MWAA is preparing a roughly $20 billion expansion to accommodate about 90 million annual passengers, more than triple current levels, under Trump-administration pressure to modernize.
source_title: MWAA almost ready to unveil Dulles expansion plan sought by Trump
supporting_excerpt: The plan envisions ultimately accommodating 90 million passengers annually—more than triple current levels... Estimates range 'up to and over $20 billion'... Master plan adopted: July 2025... Airlines concurred: July 15, 2026.
caveat: Passenger and cost figures are planning estimates reported in local press, not audited figures. Supports the argument that airfield-critical land should be protected for the expansion MWAA just committed to.

claim: The U.S. Department of Transportation holds title to Dulles land; MWAA operates the airport under a federal lease authorized by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Act of 1986, executed June 7, 1987, and extended so it now runs to 2100.
supporting_excerpt: On June 7, 1987, Washington Dulles International and Washington National Airports were transferred to the Airports Authority under a 50-year lease authorized by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Act of 1986... the Federal government holds title to the lease... in 2024, it was extended an additional 33 years... the Airports Authority's lease of the Airports will expire in 2100.
caveat: Because the land is federally owned, Section 163's carve-out preserving FAA authority over federally conveyed/acquired land and the Dec 2023 FAA land-use policy apply with full force.

claim: The Trump administration's DOT (Secretary Sean Duffy) launched an initiative and RFI to revitalize/modernize Dulles, adding federal political pressure on MWAA's capital priorities.
source_title: Trump's Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Launches New Initiative to Revitalize Dulles Airport
supporting_excerpt: Secretary Duffy initiative to revitalize Washington Dulles International Airport; related US DOT Request for Information (IAD RFI).
caveat: Reinforces that federal attention is on airfield capacity/modernization, strengthening the case against sterilizing airfield land for non-aeronautical use.
